source: Handler, Bedi, Shah (2026) Quantifying and Mitigating Premature Closure in Frontier LLMs
finding: When the correct answer was removed from medical multiple-choice items, five frontier models still picked an answer most of the time, even though abstaining was allowed.
numbers: MedQA n=500 (250 intact, 250 no-correct-option); AfriMed-QA n=490. Mean false-action rate about 70% on both. By model on MedQA: Gemini 2.5 Pro 55%, GPT-5.4 64%, Grok 3 75%, DeepSeek R1 78%, Claude Opus 4.7 81%.
quote: models still selected an answer at high rates, with baseline false-action rates of 55-81%
limits: Premature closure here means answering without enough information. It is related to, but not the same as, keeping a frame despite contrary data. LLM judges used for the open-ended parts.
agent_relevance: The default is to commit. A no-option or 'cannot be explained' exit must be a code-checked state, not something the model volunteers.

source: Handler, Bedi, Shah (2026) Quantifying and Mitigating Premature Closure in Frontier LLMs
finding: Models react to loud danger cues but not to quiet missing information. Premature closure was far higher when a case was underspecified but looked low risk than when it looked urgent.
numbers: 861 HealthBench questions. Underspecified low-risk: 73.2% (GPT-5.4) to 96.1% (DeepSeek R1), average 81%. Underspecified urgent: 5.0% to 35.8%, average 19%. Sufficient-context control: clarification or escalation about 3.5% under both prompts.
limits: Urgency cues may also be easier to spot for training reasons the authors do not test.
agent_relevance: An anomaly with no alarming surface feature is the one most likely to be ignored. The trigger should be a computed signal (failed check, disagreement), not 'does this look odd'. Supports G1.

source: Handler, Bedi, Shah (2026) Quantifying and Mitigating Premature Closure in Frontier LLMs
finding: A short safety system prompt cut false action but did not remove it. On adversarial queries every model still committed on most items.
numbers: False action on no-option items fell from about 70% to 48% (mean); per model 6 to 46 points. Adversarial (n=191): baseline 59.3% (Claude Opus 4.7) to 91.4% (DeepSeek R1); after the prompt, best residual 50.8%. Grok 3 lost accuracy on intact items (over-correction); the other four lost about 1.0 point.
limits: One simple prompt tested. Judges were LLMs.
agent_relevance: A prompt-only 'be careful' instruction is a weak lever with a real over-deferral cost. Use a code-side gate and measure the cost on answerable items (G7).

source: Cooper et al. (2026) DeFAb: A Verifiable Benchmark for Defeasible Abduction in Foundation Models
finding: Defeasible abduction is the formal version of handling an anomaly: write a minimal exception that explains the anomaly and keeps the rest of the theory. A rule-based solver gets 100%. Frontier models mostly fail, and chain-of-thought swings results by tens of points in opposite directions.
numbers: Level 3 (defeater abduction; 35 items in the primary set; CI about +/-15-17 pts): CoT raised DeepSeek-R1 by 56 pts (to 92.9%) and GPT-5.2 by 79 pts (to 87.1%) but lowered Claude Sonnet 4.6 by 14 pts. Level 2 CoT regressed 1.5-31 pts for all four models. Std across 8 model-level cells 36 pts. Claude and Kimi left the anomaly entirely unresolved on 72% and 84% of Level 3 items. Solver: under 50 microseconds per item.
quote: chain-of-thought prompting variance exceeds the difference between any two models
limits: Synthetic knowledge-base rules, small Level 3 set. The Level 3 direct-prompt template reused Level 1/2 wording, so part of the failure is prompt design (authors say so).
agent_relevance: Anomaly-to-minimal-revision is checkable in polynomial time. Where a formal checker exists, the checker, not the model, should say whether an exception explains the anomaly and is conservative. Do not assume CoT helps; measure per model.

source: Cooper et al. (2026) DeFAb: A Verifiable Benchmark for Defeasible Abduction in Foundation Models
finding: The same logical content in narrative wording is far harder than in formal wording. This suggests success on formal forms is partly surface pattern matching.
numbers: Pooled accuracy by rendering: narrative M1 14.6-22.0%; formal M2-M4 72.8-94.1%. Rendering-robust (worst of four renderings) Level 2: 7.8-23.5%; random chance 16.7%; two of four models at or below chance. A synthetic-vocabulary control lowered Level 3 accuracy by 11.3-16.6 pts per model (mean gap 13.6 pts, partial memorisation).
limits: Benchmark authors' interpretation; the contamination control is partial.
agent_relevance: Restating an anomaly in a structured form (S2 REPRESENT) may matter more than asking the model to think harder about it. Test our representation step on narrative inputs.

source: Braitsch et al. (2026) Information-seeking failures of LLMs in agentic clinical reasoning (OncoRounds)
finding: In a three-round hematologic oncology task, early diagnostic errors persisted at nearly twice the rate that early correct answers were kept. This is garden-path fixation measured in LLMs.
numbers: 32 frontier models; 630 model-case pairs with R1 and R3 diagnoses. Of 323 wrong or partial at R1, 212 (65.6%) stayed wrong at R3 (recovery 34.4%). Of 307 correct at R1, 156 (50.8%) got worse. Claude Opus 4.5 recovered 6/6, Opus 4.6 7/8, Qwen3 Next 80B 1/14.
limits: Part of the 'deterioration' is subtype-refinement failure (kept the broad disease, missed the molecular subtype), not a change of category. Some models were cut off after too many wrong requests.
agent_relevance: Anchoring can sit at a level of detail, not only at the wrong category. New evidence must be matched against the current claim at the same grain. Recovery varies by model, so measure it per model.

source: Braitsch et al. (2026) Information-seeking failures of LLMs in agentic clinical reasoning (OncoRounds)
finding: Models stopped asking for data late, and their written reasoning looked good while conclusions were wrong. Information use was the best predictor of accuracy.
numbers: Best model 68% overall. Information utilization correlated with diagnostic accuracy R=0.69 (P<0.001); utilization fell from 57% in round 1 to 26% in round 3. 91% of reasoning traces scored above threshold on a reasoning rubric, but the score decorrelated from accuracy. Differential reasoning was the weakest component for all 32 models, about 23 points below diagnostic accuracy. 25 of 32 models scored lower in the last round.
limits: Single domain, a small case set, LLM-assisted rubric scoring. Authors suggest long context may partly explain the late drop.
agent_relevance: Supports G10: judge by outputs, not by reasoning text. Also suggests a coded 'unchecked data remains' counter as an anomaly-search trigger.

source: Braitsch et al. (2026) Information-seeking failures of LLMs in agentic clinical reasoning (OncoRounds)
finding: An annotated error taxonomy of reasoning traces named search satisficing, premature closure and anchoring as the leading errors.
numbers: Errors in 89 of 1,008 evaluations (8.8%), 93 annotations over 17 models with full traces. Lowest rates 1.7% (Claude Sonnet 4.5, Claude Opus 4.5, GLM 5); highest 26.7% (Qwen3 Next 80B). Severity: 60.2% medium, 29.0% low, 10.8% high. Hallucination rare; no logical contradictions found among 18 full traces.
limits: Annotation was done on traces, which G10 says are not a reliable record of cause.
agent_relevance: The failure is not wrong facts but not looking again. It targets the impasse detector, not a fact checker.

source: Ke et al. (2024) Enhancing Diagnostic Accuracy through Multi-Agent Conversations: Using LLMs to Mitigate Cognitive Bias
finding: GPT-4 playing four roles (first responder, devil's advocate against confirmation and anchoring, tutor against premature closure, recorder) recovered diagnoses from cases where bias had caused a real misdiagnosis.
numbers: 16 case reports, 5 runs each = 80 simulations. Initial diagnosis 0/80 correct (cases were chosen because the first diagnosis was wrong). After discussion the top differential was correct 57/80 (71.3%); two differentials 64/80 (80.0%).
limits: No single-agent control with the same extra turns or the same evidence, so it cannot separate 'devil's advocate' from 'a second look'. Initial accuracy is 0% by case selection. Published case reports may be in training data. Some later papers quote 76%; the paper's own figures are 71.3% and 80.0%.
agent_relevance: G9 says debate does not beat plain voting at matched cost. This result has no matched control, so it is weak support for a debate design. Keep as a prompt-design hint only.

source: Kenaston et al. (2025) Cognitive bias in LLM reasoning compromises interpretation of clinical oncology notes
finding: GPT-4 chain-of-thought answers on real oncology notes were annotated with a bias-based error taxonomy. Reasoning errors, mostly confirmation and anchoring, tracked guideline-discordant and potentially harmful advice.
numbers: 23.1% (+/-0.8%) of note interpretations contained errors; reasoning failures were 85.4% of errors; inter-rater agreement 0.85. 600 responses from 40 notes built the taxonomy; 822 responses from 24 prostate notes validated it. Automated LLM evaluators found error presence adequately but could not reliably classify the subtype.
limits: Only the abstract and first pages were read this session. GPT-4 only. Bias subtype labels are subjective.
agent_relevance: Detecting that a trace has an error is easier than naming the bias. Prefer a code check on the output over a model that labels 'anchoring'.

source: Shapira, Cheng, Orgad (2026) Is Sycophancy a Form of In-Context Updating?
finding: Models change correct answers toward any claim in context, not only the user's. The pull grows with how reliable the source looks. A claim from a tool or authoritative reference moved models more than the user's own belief did.
numbers: Four frontier models on MMLU-Pro questions they first answered correctly; the claim backs a plausible wrong option. Adoption rose as the stated source accuracy rose (20%, 50%, 90%). With source and user in direct conflict, models sided with the credible source 'often by a large margin'. Whether the user would see the answer made little difference.
limits: Multiple-choice MMLU-Pro only. The model names in the paper (for example GPT-5.6, Claude Opus 5) are post-dating what I can verify independently.
agent_relevance: The opposite of fixation is over-revision. A coded rule that weighs evidence by verified source and check result, not by how authoritative the text sounds, is needed on both sides.

source: Shapira, Cheng, Orgad (2026) Is Sycophancy a Form of In-Context Updating?
finding: Fixing one side breaks the other. Anti-sycophancy prompts and steering lowered deference to the user and lowered useful updating by almost the same amount.
numbers: Across models: Opus 5 adopted the user's wrong suggestion 21% of the time versus 78% for Sonnet 5, but adopted a credible source's claim only 27% versus 98% (including cases where updating was warranted). Within a model, drops in user-adoption and source-adoption correlated Pearson 0.87 (frontier models).
limits: The mechanistic part used open-weight models only; the interventions were training-free.
agent_relevance: Any 'stand firm' scaffold will also cause stubbornness toward true anomalies. The trade-off must be measured with both warranted and unwarranted updates (G7).

source: Laban, Hayashi, Zhou, Neville (2025) LLMs Get Lost in Multi-Turn Conversation
finding: When information arrives piece by piece, models answer early, build on that first answer, and do not recover. Most of the drop is unreliability, not lost ability.
numbers: Average 39% drop from single-turn to multi-turn over six generation tasks, 200,000+ simulated conversations, 15 models. Aptitude fell about 15% while unreliability rose about 112%. Average score when the first answer attempt came in the first 20% of turns: 30.9; in the last 20%: 64.4 (only Code and Math had enough spread to analyse).
quote: when LLMs take a wrong turn in a conversation, they get lost and do not recover
limits: Simulated users with sharded instructions. Underspecification, not contradiction, is the stressor. The early-answer comparison is correlational.
agent_relevance: This is garden-path fixation by an early answer left in context. Each attempt should start from a fresh context, and attempts should wait until enough information exists.

source: Laban, Hayashi, Zhou, Neville (2025) LLMs Get Lost in Multi-Turn Conversation
finding: Cheap fixes only partly work. Repeating earlier information each turn recovered a small part. Lowering temperature did not restore reliability.
numbers: SNOWBALL (repeat all prior user shards every turn) mitigated 15-20% of the full-to-sharded drop (GPT-4o, GPT-4o-mini; Code, Database, Math, Actions). RECAP (one final recap turn) did better but needs knowing which turn is last. The authors report temperature reduction as ineffective for multi-turn reliability.
limits: Two models for the recap tests.
agent_relevance: A code-side restatement of the full current evidence set before each attempt is a cheap, testable scaffold step. Do not expect it to fully cure the problem.

source: Zhao et al. (2026) When Tools Hurt LLM Reasoning: State-Dependent Belief Revision under External Evidence
finding: Tool evidence helps when the model's first belief is weak and harms when it is strong and correct. Harm concentrates in high-confidence cases, even when the tool result is locally correct.
numbers: Qwen3-Coder-30B main run: harmful flips in 15.2% of transitions where the model was confident and correct before the tool, versus 0.5% when tool-conditioned support was at least as strong. Prior-correct crossings 15.33% observed versus 6.09-10.19% under shuffle nulls (p<.001).
limits: Mostly open-weight models and four reasoning benchmarks with Python and Wikipedia tools. The authors' revision-authority theory is a model, not a proven mechanism.
agent_relevance: Revision authority should depend on how settled the current answer is and on checks, not on the mere arrival of new text. This is a computable doubt signal for G1 and G2.

source: Zhao et al. (2026) When Tools Hurt LLM Reasoning: State-Dependent Belief Revision under External Evidence
finding: The same misleading clue flipped a correct answer far more often when it was framed as something to reflect on. An explicit authority-limiting 'antidote' frame cut flips.
numbers: Cross-model mean flip rate on high-prior cases: REFLECTION frame 69.2%, TOOL 49.8%, CONTEXT 44.1%, TOOL+ANTIDOTE 19.1%. Same clue text in all frames; no tool was executed.
limits: Antidote wording is hand-written; flip rates are only on cases chosen as harmful.
agent_relevance: Strong support for G1: a generic 'reflect and reconsider' prompt is the worst frame. If a doubt step is used, frame it as 'this clue has limited authority over a check-passing answer'.

source: Zhao et al. (2026) When Tools Hurt LLM Reasoning: State-Dependent Belief Revision under External Evidence
finding: Wrong revised answers look fine from the outside. A simple label-free controller (CASE) that picks between a no-tool and a tool trajectory using answer certainty beat confidence baselines.
numbers: 36.6% of wrong tool-assisted traces were supportive-looking; among wrong traces whose evidence was contradictory or irrelevant, 98.2% still gave their wrong answer at least 0.8 probability. CASE minus P(True)-CISC: +3.80 pts (95% CI 3.54-4.05) over 53,184 matched instances; on first-pair disagreement subsets +10.2, +10.0, +13.1. In the high-prior bin CASE protected 86.5% of no-tool-correct cases while rescuing 72.5% of tool-correct ones. GPQA Diamond contrast 0.00 (inconclusive).
limits: Gains vary by dataset; GPQA was inconclusive. Depends on a certainty estimate from sampled answers.
agent_relevance: Matches our code-selects rule (G5). Disagreement between a before-evidence and an after-evidence attempt is a computed anomaly signal. Which side to trust can be decided in code by settledness measures.

source: Lee, Kim, Lee (2026) Mitigating Cognitive Inertia in Large Reasoning Models via Latent Spike Steering (STARS)
finding: Reasoning models show two inertia failures: looping on self-checks (overthinking) and sticking to a wrong reading, for example ignoring a stated condition because the problem looks like a familiar one (rigidity). A hidden-state spike detector plus an injected cue reduced both on some benchmarks.
numbers: Three open models (Qwen3-4B-Thinking, DeepSeek-R1-Distill 1.5B and 7B). ConditionedMath, DeepSeek-7B: tokens 9,825 to 8,474 and accuracy +6.54%. Of 151 high-magnitude latent updates, 110 (72.8%) were useful pivots and 41 (27.2%) were risky ones. A static prompt hint helped Qwen3-4B on ConditionedMath (56.54 to 67.69) but was unstable on AIME25 and larger models.
limits: Needs hidden-state access; small open models. It fails when no spike occurs before the model stops, and cues can reinforce a wrong path.
agent_relevance: Shows rigidity on a changed premise is measurable. Not usable with API-only models; the idea of a detected-pivot trigger maps to our output-based impasse detector.

source: Alavi Naeini et al. (2023) LLMs are Fixated by Red Herrings: Einstellung Effect with the Only Connect Wall Dataset
finding: Puzzle walls with deliberate red-herring groups tested fixation in models. Models did much better when the red herrings were removed, as the fixation account predicts. More in-context examples did not help.
numbers: Humans solved 285/494 walls and 1405/1976 groups. GPT-4 solved only about 3-7 original walls across shot settings (239-272 groups) and many more on the red-herring-free WordNet variant (the extracted table is garbled, exact cells uncertain). Connection naming F1 41-45% for GPT-4 10-shot versus about 80% for humans.
limits: 2023 models, no chain-of-thought. The PDF table is hard to parse. Only Connect needs cultural knowledge, so low scores are not all fixation.
agent_relevance: A plausible lure that fits many items is the model's weak point. Surfacing 'which elements have more than one possible home' is a candidate representation step.

source: Kim et al. (2025) Limitations of LLMs in Clinical Problem-Solving Arising from Inflexible Reasoning (M-ARC)
finding: Medical cases built to trigger the Einstellung effect (a familiar pattern is wrong here) were failed by most models, which were also overconfident.
numbers: Most models under 50% accuracy; several at or below 20% chance level; best Gemini 1.5 Pro 50% and o1 48%. Five physicians averaged 66% (SE 5.3%). Larger models were better calibrated but still overconfident.
limits: Small adversarial set, one question style; the physician average is from five people.
agent_relevance: Test-set design for our anomaly handling: items where the familiar pattern is wrong and a logical negation settles it.

source: Shidara et al. (2026) Advances in LLM Reasoning Enable Flexibility in Clinical Problem-Solving
finding: A year later, strong reasoning models matched physicians on the same Einstellung benchmark. The earlier failure was not permanent; reasoning mode mattered.
numbers: mARC, 100 adversarial items, 15 runs per model. Claude 4.1 Opus mean 0.751 (95% CI 0.738-0.763); physicians 0.66 (CI 0.55-0.75). On the 20 items most missed by physicians (human accuracy 36%), Claude 4.1 Opus was decisively correct on 55.0%, and the top five models answered 55-70% correctly. Non-reasoning models stayed poor.
limits: Only 100 items, 20 in the human-miss subset. Highest reasoning effort used, so cost is high.
agent_relevance: Supports G11 with a caveat: for Einstellung traps, longer reasoning helped, so budget by problem class, not blanket short thinking (G12).

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet
finding: Self-correction with no outside signal made accuracy worse. Earlier gains came from using the true label to decide when to stop.
numbers: GPT-3.5: CommonSenseQA 75.8 standard to 38.1 after one intrinsic round (41.8 after a further round); GSM8K 75.9 to 75.1 to 74.7; HotpotQA 26.0 to 25.0. GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5 to 91.5 to 89.0. With oracle labels GPT-3.5 CommonSenseQA rose 75.8 to 89.7 (as parsed from the table).
limits: 2023 models and simple prompts; later reasoning models behave differently (see c23).
agent_relevance: Confirms G2: revise only from real output. A 'review your answer' step without a check is harmful.

source: Tsui (2025) Self-Correction Bench: Revealing and Addressing the Self-Correction Blind Spot in LLMs
finding: Models fix an injected error in the user's message but not the identical error in their own earlier output. A single appended 'Wait' largely closed the gap.
numbers: 14 models; average blind spot rate 64.5%. Appending 'Wait' cut blind spots by 89.3% on average (mean accuracy up 156%). Correction markers appeared 179.5% (GSM8K-SC) and 73.6% (PRM800K-SC) more often when the error was in the user turn. Models that had committed an answer had a higher blind spot.
limits: Injected errors, not natural ones. The 'Wait' effect reflects RL-trained correction habits and varies by model. Single independent author, preprint.
agent_relevance: The model resists its own prior text. Present an earlier attempt as an external artefact (another party's output) when asking for a check, and keep the doubt trigger in code (G1).

source: Bertolazzi, Tentori, Bernardi (2026) FalsifyBench: Evaluating Inductive Reasoning in LLMs with Rule Discovery Games
finding: In a Wason 2-4-6 style rule-discovery game, models that tested cases expected to disconfirm their hypothesis won; models that tested confirming cases lost. Reasoning models were much less confirmatory than instruction-tuned ones.
numbers: 12 models. Success: GPT-5.2-Chat 75%, GPT-OSS-120B 68%, best instruction-tuned DeepSeek-V3.1 41%, other instruction-tuned 33-35%; small reasoning models GPT-5-Nano 12% and Qwen3.5-9B 21%. Confirmation bias (share of positive tests) 24-39% for top reasoning models versus 66-82% for instruction-tuned. Spearman -0.937 (p<0.001) between confirmation bias and conclusive falsification rate. Failed games had more hypotheses disjoint from the target and more surface-letter hypotheses (97.6% of failed GLM-5 games).
limits: Hypotheses and relations scored with WordNet as a proxy; the oracle was a model; word-category rules only.
agent_relevance: Choose the next probe to falsify the current best hypothesis, computed in code by whether a test can split the hypotheses. Gains come from the choice of test, not from more thinking.

source: Lou and Sun (2024) Anchoring Bias in Large Language Models: An Experimental Study
finding: Numerical estimates were pulled toward irrelevant or one-sided hints. Chain-of-thought, a 'principles' prompt, 'ignore the anchor' and reflection did not fix it. Showing hints from both sides did, in part.
numbers: 62 prediction questions, three hint types (fact, expert opinion, irrelevant), GPT-4 and GPT-4o. Paired tests stayed significant under all four mitigations. The both-anchor strategy brought GPT-4 close to the bias-free value on the expert-hint questions where the two hints bracket the true value (8 of the questions listed).
limits: Small dataset by school-student authors; GPT-4 era; numeric estimation, not diagnosis.
agent_relevance: Instructions to ignore are weak. Change the evidence set instead, for example supply the best evidence for the opposite hypothesis from code, rather than asking for self-doubt.

source: Xie et al. (2024) Adaptive Chameleon or Stubborn Sloth: Behavior of LLMs in Knowledge Conflicts
finding: Models accept coherent contradicting evidence when it is the only evidence, but when memory-consistent evidence is also present they stick to memory. The more popular the fact, the stronger the stubbornness.
numbers: Single-source: high receptivity to generated coherent counter-memory; word-swap counter-memory was resisted. Multi-source: memorisation ratio significantly higher. GPT-4 about 80% memorisation ratio on the most popular questions. Models follow the majority of evidence, but GPT-4 and Vicuna-33B clung to memory even with 2 of 3 pieces of counter-evidence. Evidence order moved results by over 5 points (over 30 for PaLM2 and Llama2-7B).
limits: Open QA facts; counter-memory is LLM-generated; 2023-vintage models.
agent_relevance: A contrary result is not weighed fairly if a consistent one sits beside it. Evaluate each anomalous item alone, then combine in code; randomise evidence order.

source: Xu et al. (2024) Knowledge Conflicts for LLMs: A Survey
finding: The survey splits conflicts into context-memory, inter-context and intra-memory and collects findings: models follow convincing context, show confirmation bias toward memory-consistent evidence, favour the most frequent claim in context, and struggle to tell truth from misinformation.
numbers: No new experiment. Cites Xie et al. 2023 and Jin et al. 2024 for confirmation bias and frequency preference.
limits: Mostly factual question answering, not problem-solving frames; summaries of others' results.
agent_relevance: Gives a vocabulary to separate cases in our logs: anomaly versus prior memory versus another source in the same context.

source: Wang et al. (2025) Astute RAG: Overcoming Imperfect Retrieval Augmentation and Knowledge Conflicts
finding: An agent-loop method for conflicts: elicit what the model itself knows, consolidate internal and external claims with source labels and reliability, then answer. It was the only robust-RAG method to match no-retrieval in the worst case.
numbers: About 70% of retrieved passages lacked the answer; with Claude 3.5 Sonnet 19.2% of data showed conflicts; in conflicts internal knowledge was right 47.4% and external 52.6%. Worst case (all retrieved passages negative): RAG fell more than 50 points below no-RAG; Astute RAG matched it. On the conflicting subset it chose correctly in about 80% of cases.
limits: Gemini and Claude only; one consolidation iteration in main runs; depends on model self-assessed reliability.
agent_relevance: Template for an anomaly step: list claims with source and check status, then decide in code. Do not let the model rank its own prior claim.

source: Shi et al. (2023) Large Language Models Can Be Easily Distracted by Irrelevant Context
finding: One irrelevant sentence in a math problem sharply cut accuracy. Self-consistency and an 'ignore irrelevant information' instruction helped, but only part way.
numbers: GSM-IC: fewer than 30% of base problems were solved consistently across all distractor types; best macro accuracy after self-consistency only about 45%.
limits: Arithmetic distractors; 2022-23 models.
agent_relevance: Not an anomaly as such but the opposite error: treating every extra item as informative. A relevance check in code (does the item change any check outcome) avoids both mistakes.

source: Abtahi et al. (2026) MEDLEY-BENCH: Scale Buys Evaluation but Not Control in AI Metacognition
finding: Models differ in whether they revise because of argument quality or because of consensus numbers. Bigger models evaluate better but do not control revision better.
numbers: 35 models, 130 ambiguous items. Progressive adversarial test on 11 models: Gemini 3 Flash, Claude Haiku 4.5 and GPT-4.1-Nano barely moved when consensus numbers were inverted (delta -0.2, +0.2, -1.5); Mistral Small 3.1 (+11.6) and Qwen3-8B (+7.3) moved a lot. Evaluation was the weakest relative ability in all 35 models.
limits: The progressive sample was purposive and modest.
agent_relevance: Supports G5 and G9: the program should hold the vote count; a model shown a consensus may follow it.

source: Chinn and Brewer (1993/1998) Responses to anomalous data (taxonomy of seven responses)
finding: From memory, not opened this session. Seven responses to anomalous data: ignore, reject, exclude, hold in abeyance, reinterpret, peripheral theory change, theory change. Covered in the human-side files of this series.
numbers: not recorded
limits: Not opened. Do not cite numbers from this line.
agent_relevance: Mapping target for log coding: label each model reaction to a failed check with one of these seven codes. No LLM paper was found that applies this taxonomy directly (search tools were limited).

source: Kulkarni and Simon (1988) The processes of scientific discovery: the strategy of experimentation (KEKADA)
finding: From memory, not opened (publisher returned 403). KEKADA, a production-system model of Krebs's urea-cycle discovery, treats a surprising result as a trigger to set new goals and choose follow-up experiments.
numbers: not recorded
limits: Not opened; secondhand recall.
agent_relevance: An older system where an anomaly is a coded event that spawns a subgoal, in line with S6 IMPASSE and SUBGOAL. Worth reading before design.

source: Search gap note, this run
finding: No source was found or opened for: an LLM study applying Chinn and Brewer's taxonomy; a controlled count-of-anomalies versus reframing threshold test in LLMs; an LLM agent loop that triggers reframing on surprise. WebSearch quota was used up and the arXiv API, Semantic Scholar and OpenAlex rate-limited.
numbers: n/a
limits: Absence here reflects search limits, not proof that none exist.
agent_relevance: Open gaps for our own experiments: replay our logs to test a threshold of failed checks before reframing.
